articles.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty
articles.author: Shannon Gibson, Professor of Environmental Studies, Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment.
It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way.

Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions. Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths.
The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs.
These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference, being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia.

In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive.
The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation.

Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions.
Deciding which species deserve protection
An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets.

Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods.

Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services. Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings.

Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat, helping other species living there.

A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding, despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing.

Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss.
At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say?

While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection, but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too.

Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai, Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported.

Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions.

At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories.

The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last.

Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated.

The global biodiversity framework calls for a “whole-of-society” approach, recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power.

Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not.

The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible.
Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.

articles.title: Is it wrong to kill wild animals that attack humans? Sometimes conservation demands it
articles.author: Adam Hart, Professor of Conservation Ecology, University of Gloucestershire
paras: When an Amur tiger recently killed a man at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in northern England, the park announced that the tiger would not be killed.
Days later, a 71-year-old fisherman was killed by an alligator in Florida in the US. This time, the animal was captured and killed.

Two fatal attacks, but two very different responses. The distinction is not simply between a tiger in captivity and an alligator in the wild. It is about whether killing an animal can prevent further harm.

Sometimes removing a dangerous animal is necessary to protect human life. More surprisingly, it can also protect other wildlife, by preventing people retaliating against animals who weren’t involved in the original attack.

A tiger attacking someone who enters its enclosure is behaving like a tiger, and killing it would achieve nothing. Removing an animal posing an ongoing threat is different. But in Yorkshire, the tiger remains behind barriers designed to keep people safe. The fatal encounter needs investigating, but the problem was that a person got in, not that a tiger got out. Killing the tiger would not address any potential failures in enclosure security.

The Florida alligator presents a different problem. There is no good evidence that crocodilians develop a particular taste for human flesh after an attack, but they can become accustomed to people and learn to associate human activity with food, potentially increasing the risk of further encounters.

Where an animal poses a continuing threat, removing it may be justified on safety grounds, although a fatal attack alone does not establish that killing it was necessary. For communities that depend on crocodile-inhabited rivers for fishing, washing or collecting water, simply telling people to avoid them may not be realistic.

In Borneo, a fatal attack by a false gharial, a large and threatened relative of crocodiles, prompted a search for the animal responsible. A large male was killed, but examination of its stomach failed to establish that it was responsible.
Following another fatal attack, a second false gharial was killed, this time with the victim’s remains in its stomach. No further crocodilians were killed following that incident.

The consequences of indiscriminate retaliation can be devastating. In 2018, after a man was killed by a crocodile at a breeding facility in West Papua, Indonesia, an angry crowd entered the facility and killed all 292 crocodiles kept there, including hundreds of animals that had played no part in the attack.

When people fear that a dangerous animal remains a threat, the pressure to act can be considerable. If authorities fail to respond, communities may take matters into their own hands, killing animals uninvolved in the attack. Identifying and removing the responsible individual can sometimes prevent this escalation and protect other wildlife.

But targeted removal is not straightforward, not least because identifying the right animal can be difficult. In addition, involvement in a fatal attack does not necessarily mean an individual is unusually dangerous. The circumstances may explain what happened, and killing the animal may do little to prevent another attack.

Such retaliation is not confined to crocodiles. In India in 2024, villagers near Ranthambore tiger reserve killed a tiger following the death of a shepherd. That year, a leopard that injured four people in Karnataka, south-west India, was beaten to death by a crowd, despite wildlife officials attempting to capture it.

Retaliation also occurs when lions kill livestock. In Kenya in 2015, herders poisoned a cow carcass after lions killed their cattle. Three lions from the famous Marsh Pride died, along with 11 vultures.

The incident illustrates how livestock conflict can become a wider conservation problem. A timely, targeted response may be preferable to allowing fear and anger to escalate into indiscriminate killing.

Often, better barriers, safer access to water or changes in how people encounter wildlife offer more lasting solutions. Providing safe water, for example, reduces the need to enter crocodile-inhabited rivers. Killing an animal should never be a substitute for addressing the circumstances that made an attack possible.

For people living alongside dangerous wildlife, these are not abstract conservation dilemmas. Expecting communities to tolerate serious risks without effective protection is neither reasonable nor fair. Those communities also need a meaningful say in how dangerous animals are managed. Decisions made solely by distant authorities or conservation organisations can overlook both the risks people face and the practical options available to them.

Equally, killing an animal does not necessarily make anyone safer. Decisions should depend on whether removal is likely to reduce danger and protect other wildlife. Sometimes killing a dangerous animal is justified, not despite conservation concerns, but because of them.

articles.title: Subsidence claims: after drought, ground can shrink, swell or even collapse when it rains – causing damage to homes
articles.author: Arya Assadi Langroudi, Senior Lecturer in Geotechnical Engineering, University of East London
paras: A crack appears beside a window after weeks of scorching weather. As much as you might hope the ground beneath your house will recover with the first rain, the effects of a dry summer can continue long after temperatures fall.

The UK is recovering from the hottest summer on record. The drought, however, has not simply disappeared. According to the Environment Agency, south-east England received 61% of its normal September rainfall, leaving its soil moisture deficit around twice the seasonal average.

The financial consequences are staggering. After the UK’s 2022 heatwave, insurers recorded 18,000 claims from homeowners in the second half of that year for subsidence (the gradual sinking of the ground surface).

In 2025, domestic subsidence payouts reached £307 million, 10% above 2024 figures. Between April and June 2026, the average paid claim reached £20,000. Although payouts include repair costs, the amount shows the scale of the damage to houses by climate change.

Clay-rich soils commonly lose water and contract during drought. If that happens unevenly beneath a foundation, one part of a house may settle further than another, producing cracks in its walls. Trees may intensify local drying as their thirsty roots extract water from the ground.

When rain replenishes moisture, some clays swell again, potentially pushing foundations upward. The recovery, however, is neither complete nor instantaneous. A heavy shower may wet the surface without restoring moisture several metres below ground, and different parts of a building may move at different rates.

Cycles of drought and rain can displace salt and sticky clays within sandy soils and clay-like silty soils. While that displacement generally makes these soils stiffer, it can also make them susceptible to sudden subsidence when large volumes of water flow through the pores opened up after the summer drought, weakening the contacts holding the grains apart.

These soils can show problems normally associated with “collapsible soils”, which are explored in my 2019 study of English loess, a fine, wind-blown silty sediment that’s very porous. My research shows that seemingly similar silty soils can behave quite differently, depending on how they formed and how their particles became arranged and bonded over time. Some layers are better at supporting loads than others.

Where soils are susceptible to collapse once wet, rapid subsidence may be further escalated by a leaking drain or poorly sited soakaway (an underground drainage system that collects surface rainwater, stores it and allows for it to slowly seep out). That is one of the principal reasons the British Geological Survey (BGS) advises maintaining water pipes and keeping soakaways further from buildings where loosely cemented soils and soluble rocks may be present.

Two houses on the same street may not respond in the same way. Their foundations may reach different depths or sit on different soil layers. The ground beneath one garden may be shaded by trees, while the next has been paved over. Rainwater can be diverted by a driveway, concentrated by a leaking pipe, or drawn away by roots.
A geological map can flag a potential hazard, but it cannot tell a homeowner whether a particular crack is caused by ground movement. The building, soil and local water conditions all affect that.
Soil is not simply a platform for foundations. Its pores store nutrients and water for plants, lock carbon, carry rain towards groundwater and provide habitats for roots, fungi and earthworms.

Roots are part of the soil’s plumbing. They create pathways for water and hold particles in place. If drought damages fine roots or kills vegetation, the ground may absorb rainfall differently, while its surface becomes more exposed to erosion.

A 2025 review of drought-affected soil studies by the BGS describes how drying may reduce microbial and earthworm activity, weaken soil structure and expose bare ground as plants die back. This makes some soils at a greater risk of erosion by the runoff when rain returns. Soil staying wet for a long time, combined with intense rainfall can increase the erosion risk.

Soil degradation, loss and erosion can affect the food security. In the 2026 harvest survey, UK wheat yields were around 11% below their five-year average and spring barley around 17% below. Some crops like oilseed rape, enjoyed higher yield. The contrasting yields mark why one harsh summer does not produce one uniform outcome across the landscape.

So what should homeowners do to manage the problem? Many fine plaster cracks are cosmetic. New or widening diagonal cracks, cracks visible inside and outside, suddenly sticking doors or distorted floors merit closer attention. Photograph them with a ruler and date, check that gutters and drains are sound, and seek advice from your insurer and a qualified surveyor if movement appears to be progressing. Do not rush to remove a mature tree: it may change the moisture balance and create a different problem.

The longer-term outlook makes better ground management urgent. The BGS estimates that, by 2070, more than 1.8 million British properties could be in areas where clay is particularly prone to shrinking and swelling. This figure assumes a medium level of future greenhouse gas emissions. If emissions remain high, the number could rise to 4.2 million properties are at risk. This does not mean all these homes will suffer damage. The figures identify potentially vulnerable ground, rather than predict actual subsidence. They also exclude other hazards, such as the sudden collapse of some soils once flooded.

Protecting homes is not just about building stronger foundations. It calls for careful drainage, sensible land and tree management plus healthy soils that can retain and carry water without creating new hazards elsewhere.
Arya Assadi Langroudi receives funding from Royal Academy of Engineering.

articles.title: The driveway divide: why parking for electric vehicles is such a big barrier
articles.author: Bernardino D'Amico, Professor, School of Computing, Engineering and the Built Environment, Edinburgh Napier University
paras: Most people who have an electric car have access to a driveway or private parking. In England, 90% EV owners can park easily and charge theirs from home. But roughly 40% of UK households don’t have off-street parking, so the question is how they would charge an EV and would easy access to home-charging influence their decision to acquire one.

The practical problems are well documented. In a block of flats or a tenement, installing an EV charger may not be an option due to the cost and the legal consent required from third parties who may have no interest in giving it. In a block of flats, installing an EV charger can also be difficult because it may require running cables from the flat’s electricity supply to a shared parking space, if one is available, or to the street where the vehicle is parked.

This can involve drilling through walls, installing cables through shared areas of the building and altering existing electrical infrastructure. Such work is generally more complex (and costly) than in a detached house, where a charger can usually be installed on an external wall close to the property’s electricity supply.

According to the Electric Vehicle Association, a non-profit representing EV drivers in England, 87% of EV owners with driveways say their car is cheaper to run than a petrol or diesel equivalent. Among those without, only half say the same because they have to default to more expensive public chargers.

As a researcher exploring effective designs for urban environments, I’ve been looking at whether fixing this home-charging gap would solve the problem of access. I found that the driveway divide is really less about infrastructure and actually more about wealth in disguise.

My colleagues and I looked at data on Scottish households. Our latest study suggests that having a driveway does not get you into the electric car market – money does. A driveway only helps once you are already in.

We linked nationally representative Scottish household and housing data sets, capturing variables such as income, work, dwelling home type and age, and whether anyone there already owns or intends to buy an EV. Then we built a causal model: think of it as a map of factors that genuinely influence each other.

Wealthier households are far more likely to live in a house that comes with a driveway and to also have the financial means to buy an electric car. A standard statistical model cannot tell those two things apart. It will simply report that driveways and electric cars “go together” or correlate, leaving researchers like me to guess why.

Our approach let us ask a question you cannot normally answer from survey data: what would actually change if a household suddenly had a private driveway, holding everything else the same? The answer surprised us.

Having a driveway does make a difference. It raises the probability of owning an electric car by 70%, a substantial jump for a group (the EV owners) that is relatively small to begin with. Immediate intent to buy an EV rises too, but almost all of that effect lands on households already thinking about buying an electric car at some point in the future. A driveway pushes people along a journey they had already started.

For the roughly half of Scottish households not considering to buy an electric car at all, a driveway changes almost nothing. Income, on the other hand, is different: when we simulated what would happen if a household earned more, the share of households not considering buying an electric car fell by 23%, that is more than ten times the apparent driveway effect on that group.

The contrast is stark: money opens the door, a driveway walks you to the till. The two factors operate at different stages, which explains something that has puzzled researchers. Electric car uptake has been slowest among people in flats and tenements, and the natural conclusion has been that home charging is the problem. Our findings suggest that is only true for people already considering to buy an EV, whether sooner or later.

A Glasgow tenement household that has decided to go electric but has nowhere to charge from home faces a real infrastructural barrier. For a household on a modest income that has never seriously considered buying an electric car, the main barrier may instead be the upfront cost. Although average advertised prices for new EVs have recently fallen below those of petrol cars, this does not mean that comparable cars cost the same. At the more affordable end of the market, new EVs still tend to be less affordable than new petrol or diesel cars.
Making street charging more accessible or public charging cheaper could help households who can afford an EV. It would not, however, solve the problem of being able to afford one in the first place.

All of this points to a two-track policy response. For households outside the EV market, the priority is affordability: a stronger used electric car market, and financial support aimed at those who need it rather than those already buying in. For households already intending to buy but stuck without a driveway, home-charging access is the binding constraint.

Scotland is already piloting cross-pavement charging, which runs a cable gully under the pavement so a car parked on the street can be charged from the house. The Scottish government has also consulted on relaxing planning rules to make on-street charging easier.

The driveway divide is real, but it also involves a wealth divide. Any equitable transition needs to tackle both. Investing in home-charging infrastructure alone will mainly benefit the people who were already going to buy an electric car anyway.

articles.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
articles.author: Kayla Morton, Assistant Professor of Blue Economy and Policy, University of Delaware
paras: A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate. But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris. It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions, primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.
Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.
While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts.

Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.
Benefits of federal investment

Elected officials are sometimes accused of “pork barrel politics,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.

Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.”

That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.
The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election
Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election.

During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “economic development opportunities,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself.

Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.

In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.
We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022.

When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.

Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.
These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.

While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.
Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks

Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases.
The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands.

This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.

These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.

articles.title: Why and how US and Canadian energy markets are so deeply intertwined
articles.author: Stefano Tijerina, Senior Lecturer of Management, University of Maine
paras: The 50% tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration on imports from Canada in July 2026, and the reciprocal 50% tariffs imposed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s administration on imports to Canada from the U.S. a month later, do not include oil and natural gas. Electricity and some petroleum products were also left out, although they remain subject to a 10% tariff imposed in 2025.

That’s because the two countries’ energy systems and markets are so intertwined that tariffs would devastate both economies. Canada is the biggest supplier of foreign petroleum to the United States, supplying half of all its petroleum imports. It is also the only direct foreign supplier of electricity to the U.S., with 34 major transmission points moving electricity from Canada south across the border.
In truth, Canada could shut down those power links and leave thousands of Americans in the dark, as Ontario provincial Premier Doug Ford threatened in August 2026.

But researchers like me, who study the historical links that have shaped Canadian and U.S. business relations, know that over the past 50 years Canada has expanded its energy production with one specific goal: serving U.S. consumption. In 2024, 84% of Canadian oil production and 76% of Canadian electricity production were exported to the U.S. Without American buyers, there is no real energy market in Canada.

Since the second half of the 19th century, energy generated on both sides of the border – and across them – has connected the two nations. The Great Lakes Basin was the hydraulic center of energy interconnectivity, as both nations shared the energy generated by Niagara Falls and the St. Lawrence River.

During the early stages of World War II, even before the U.S. entered the fight, Canada and the U.S. started to integrate their energy systems. That work was part of joint security efforts to protect North America through the integration of defense manufacturing production systems.

The Ogdensburg Declaration of 1940 and the 1941 Hyde Park Declaration consolidated and formalized the strategic economic and military cooperation between the two countries and set the foundations for future collaboration.
From cooperation to integration
After the war, Canadian and U.S. businesses liked the idea of sharing production and manufacturing operations, even beyond war-related work.

Nevertheless, manufacturing on both sides of the border went back to prewar ways of producing things domestically. Nationalist voices opposed the idea of further integrating the Canadian and U.S. economies.

Less than two decades after the war ended, though, the two nations signed the Auto Pact of 1965, which eliminated tariffs on cars, trucks and automotive parts. Canadian parts manufacturers could compete directly with those based in the U.S., all to serve U.S. automakers.
This initial experiment in free trade revealed to businesses on both sides of the border that supply chain integration could benefit other production and service industries.

By 1989, the two countries had signed a full-scale free trade agreement that removed tariffs for goods crossing the border in either direction. That opened the door for more closely integrating their energy markets too.

In 1992, a U.S. federal law changed a wide swath of regulations over the country’s energy markets. Some of the provisions allowed Canadian companies to sell excess energy to the U.S., and two years later the North American Free Trade Agreement brought Mexico into the relationship too.
NAFTA integrated the production, processing and distribution of thousands of goods and services across all three countries.

But it was the interconnection of energy infrastructure that turned the Canadian and U.S. economies into one single energy market. Today, four major U.S. electrical grids depend on imported power from Canada: those serving the six New England states, New York state, 15 states across the Midwest and the South, and California.

Moreover, there are more than 40 natural gas and petroleum liquids pipelines connecting Canada with the United States. And although energy products move back and forth across the border, the U.S. has an energy trade deficit with Canada. Much of the U.S. economy runs on Canadian energy, and much of Canada’s energy production is sold to the U.S.
The current reality on the ground shows an integrated energy system between the two nations: something very difficult and costly to untangle, and a process that would take decades to reengineer.
Today, those links form the basis for very tight integration between the two countries’ business and industrial marketplaces.
For example, Maine, where I live and work, gets close to 30% of its electricity from Canada.
The state’s northern electrical grid is run by the New Brunswick Power Corp., owned by the province of New Brunswick, which serves close to 60,000 Mainers.

Today, Maine’s electric grid is owned mostly by foreign interests, including ENMAX, the municipally owned utilities corporation of Calgary, Alberta, and the owner of Versant Power, which serves 16% of Maine’s market. And 80% is served by Central Maine Power, which is owned by Iberdrola from Spain.

Canadian energy reaches deeper into the U.S., too. In 2025, Hydro-Quebec, a company that generates electricity from dams across the province of Quebec, secured a deal with local regulators to use Maine as a corridor to supply clean energy to Massachusetts. Hydro-Quebec is owned by the government of the province of Quebec.
The bilateral integration of energy infrastructure over the past 30-plus years explains why this sector was exempt from the most recent tariffs.

articles.title: How candidates are (quietly) talking about climate change – 3 election strategies you’ll see across the US
articles.author: Geoffrey Henderson, Assistant Professor, School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan
paras: Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days. But polls show the majority of voters in 2026 are also concerned about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise.
So why are fewer candidates talking openly about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than just a few years ago?
At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, we study climate communication and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns.

Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to fill up their cars, pay their electric bills and insure their homes against hurricanes and wildfires. It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war.

Fossil fuel industry interests have long sought to polarize the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in his new book, “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change.
When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies.
The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels.

Many have been painting data centers, rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains. Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates. They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to bring their own energy sources onto the grid.

In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S. Senate, emphasizes lowering energy and utility costs. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “higher electric rates.”

Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that climate change messages can alienate swing voters, who prioritize affordability.

If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both Brown and Cooper have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies.
Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election. However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past.

In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “bold action to invest in clean energy” if reelected in November. In Maine, Senate candidate Troy Jackson asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice.

Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that candidates should link higher costs to climate change, such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk. He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – namely, solar and wind power – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence.

If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change. However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges.
The all-of-the-above proponents

Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways. They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs. Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use cuts against global climate goals.

Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative. These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose “all of the above” energy strategy espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions.

In Iowa, U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled extreme weather is raising insurance costs. But he has also focused on lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel. James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by boosting renewable energy while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources.

These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels. Turek and Talarico are both running in states with abundant wind power.
Where are the voters on this issue?
Studies from the U.S. and Germany find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change.
So how well do candidates’ platforms represent today’s voters?

Yale’s spring 2026 survey found that 49% of voters believe global warming should be a high priority for Congress and the president. But 70% of moderate or conservative Democrats share this view, alongside 84% of liberal Democrats. Even 1 in 3 liberal-to-moderate Republicans considers the climate a high priority.

Yet polling also suggests that other issues, such as the increasing cost of living, are even more important to many voters. This data suggests that pro-climate messages could appeal to swing voters most strongly if climate policies are seen as complementary to affordability.

Still, a recent survey shows that voters open to Democratic candidates are more likely to support a candidate who prioritizes climate change. Climate messaging may especially resonate with young voters. Over a third of those ages 18 to 29 in a recent Harvard Youth Poll considered climate change an urgent national crisis. Young Republicans are more supportive of addressing climate change than their older counterparts.

While many shifts in the way candidates talk about climate policy have little impact on people’s willingness to participate in collective efforts to address it, messages emphasizing cost savings durably increase support for renewable energy across party lines. Voters’ current concerns about inflation could make climate messages involving affordability especially effective in 2026, though the impact of these messages may vary from state to state.
Retail politics and the way forward

These different approaches reflect the Democratic Party’s efforts to build a “big tent” that can attract voters with a wide range of views and priorities. Yet Democrats are generally coalescing around a message designed to appeal to working-class voters: that Trump and the Republicans are raising your cost of living.
November’s midterm elections will offer some insight into whether Democrats’ energy affordability message will resonate in the 2028 presidential election.
Geoffrey Henderson has worked on a project that received funding from the National Science Foundation.
Nathaniel Geiger has received funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Phoebe Giannisi’s eco-poetry challenges the idea that humans are separate from nature
articles.author: Laura Jansen, Associate Professor in Classics & Comparative Literature, University of Bristol
paras: For decades, data has told the story of our ecological crisis. Scientists track carbon emissions, map deforestation and log biodiversity loss. Yet data alone cannot make humanity feel the reality of a changing planet. True impact hinges on a shift in language – a vocabulary that dissolves the border between the human and the living world.

Phoebe Giannisi embodies this shift. Poet, classicist, performer, architect and environmentalist, Giannisi has produced one of the most radical bodies of eco-poetry in contemporary literature. Her work blends ancient Greek myth, site-specific performance, video poems and field recordings to offer a long-lasting lesson in what it means to coexist on a vulnerable earth.

Giannisi’s environmental message is anchored in the chimera. In classical mythology, the chimera was a fire-breathing monster, part lion, part goat, part serpent. For Giannisi, this creature is not a monstrous abstraction but a biological and ethical reality.

In her collection Chimera (2024), Giannisi bridges ancient myth with modern genetics, drawing a line from Homer’s legendary she-goat chimera to the scientific phenomenon of microchimerism – the way cells from one organism can live permanently inside another. Humans are, her poetry suggests, inherently collaborative creatures. As she writes in the poem Chimera II:
Call me Chimera. A being composed of other beings A being with different genetic codes incorporated. Various genes connected in one body. Multiple body.

Giannisi’s poetry challenges the delusion that humans stand apart from nature, either as masters or saviours. Instead, she invites her readers to recognise that we are composite creatures, physically and ecologically tangled with the world around us. To harm the landscape is to tear apart our own multi-species body.

This philosophy comes to life through Giannisi’s use of multiple voices. Her poems, now collected in Goatsong (2025), abandon the solitary narrator to thrive as living ecosystems where human and non-human voices hold equal weight. In her second poetry collection, Cicada (2022), the protagonist is the eponymous insect. Giannisi layers ancient texts by Plato, Archilochus and the Japanese poet Bashō, alongside observations of the insect’s life cycle and its droning mating calls. Its song becomes environmental testimony – a non-human language demanding the reader’s attention.

Giannisi’s focus deepened in Chimera, her third collection. In it, she tracks the ancient traditions of northern Greece’s Vlach herding communities, who move their livestock seasonally between mountain and valley pastures.

Rather than romanticising pastoral life, Giannisi constructs an archive of shared survival, reassembling state archives, regional oral histories and her own field recordings. In her live performances, Giannisi loops the cries of shepherds alongside the bellowing of the herd, the roar of a passing motorcycle and the grinding crunch of a cement mixer.

This acoustic space forces listeners to inhabit the modern industrial world and the ancient, animal landscape simultaneously. It is an ecology of sound that captures both the beauty of shared life and the vulnerability of an environment under threat.
Language as a material path

Trained as an architect, Giannisi conceives of language as a physical path to be walked, tasted and felt. When I hosted Giannisi at the Center of Hellenic Studies, Harvard in October 2023, I watched this spatial approach to poetry take shape in the room. There is an intimate, architectural precision to how she moves language off the page and into a shared physical space.

For her 2017 installation Aigis II at the Panourgias Museum in Amfissa, Greece, Giannisi inscribed her poetry onto semitransparent goatskin parchment. On one side, she traced traditional migration routes and on the other, she wrote lines of verse. As I observed viewers handling the parchment, the written word and the geography of the earth ghost one another through the animal hide.

In this method of composition, the human body becomes the primary medium for environmental memory. In her performances, Giannisi routinely blocks her own sight with a cloth or basket, intentionally de-centering her own human gaze to open up a vulnerable, sensory relationship with her surroundings. Her poems are filled with the taste of an earthy cicada, the sting of sea salt and the pungent smell of animal secretions.

This late autumn, that physical performance of environmental memory is coming to the University of Bristol. I will join Giannisi and her poet-translator, Brian Sneeden, to see how these ancient textures resonate inside a new architectural space, letting our contemporary landscape and classical myth collide once again.

Grounding her poetry in these realities allows Giannisi to create a space where human and environmental forces spill into one another. This strategy carries a subtle political edge, positioning her work as a defence of the “commons”, the shared resources currently being dismantled by economic profit. Her collaborative projects, including acoustic explorations of marine soundscapes, bear witness to the devastating loss of biodiversity driven by climate change and industrial expansion.

In the boundary crossing tradition of poet and translator Barbara Köhler and the 2026 Nobel prize winner Anne Carson, Giannisi dissolves the divisions between myth, scholarship and creativity, turning them into vital tools for navigating our difficult era.

Surviving the ecological crisis requires an entirely new framework of imagination. We are called to view our world not as resources to exploit, but as a vast, connected web where every creature’s song breathes life into the whole.

articles.title: Kipper cream or fish in custard? A century of magazine recipes reveals how Britain’s seafood tastes have narrowed
articles.author: Ruth H. Thurstan, Associate Professor in Marine and Historical Ecology, University of Exeter
paras: Walk into a British supermarket and you will see prawns from south-east Asia, salmon from Norway, lobster from Canada and tuna from the Indian Ocean.
Seafood is among the most traded foods globally, yet around 80% of the seafood British consumers eat comes from just five species groups: cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns.

It’s tempting to assume Britain has long been a nation of cautious fish eaters with a few trusted favourites. Histories of certain species, such as cod (the mainstay of the national dish, fish and chips) and herring (kippers on toast, anyone?) can reinforce that narrative. But my new research exploring a century of recipes from one of Britain’s longstanding domestic magazines suggests a different story.

Records of which fish people cooked at home are surprisingly patchy. Retail data are mostly short term and commercially owned, while long-running household surveys rarely record fish to species level. National statistics track what is landed and traded, but the home kitchen, where food choices are made and lifelong habits are formed, leaves far fewer traces.

Recipes offer a window into this hidden past. They don’t measure what people ate, but they do show which fish readers were expected to recognise, be able to buy and want to cook. Britain’s fish supply and trade have changed dramatically over the past century, so I wondered whether the fish in recipes had changed too.

British Good Housekeeping magazine was first published in the 1920s and continues today as Good Housekeeping UK. Its focus on home life and steady output of recipes make it well suited to tracking changing food culture. Sampling several years per decade, I collected 1,192 fish and shellfish recipes published from 1923-2025.

Recipes published in the 1920s reflect a broad and flexible fish culture. Sole, oysters, shrimp and salmon appeared alongside halibut, lobster and herring, in dishes such as oyster cocktails with olives, kipper cream and halibut steaks in milk. Almost a third of recipes included suggestions for substitute species. Some recipes (such as fish baked in custard) simply called for fish or white fish, probably because supply was not always predictable.
From the 1950s, that flexibility gave way to more standardisation. Recipes increasingly assumed prepared fillets rather than whole fish, and frozen products became common.

The 1970s marked a turning point. From then on, cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns accounted for the most species mentions each decade, while sole, herring, oysters and lobster appeared less often. My research shows the number of fish species represented in recipes in each decade didn’t collapse, but attention became concentrated on fewer of them.

What explains the shift? Supply matters, but the picture is more complicated. Cod declined in British waters but remained a recipe staple, as distant water fleets and then imports kept it on sale. Herring and oyster populations also declined but did not disappear from markets entirely, yet they faded from the magazine’s pages. What stayed familiar depended less on what our local fleets caught than on increasingly globalised supply chains and marketing.

Within this glossy monthly magazine, at least, fish recipes are more globally adventurous than ever: recent examples include gochujang sticky cod and miso prawn skewers. Yet the fish remain largely the same five. Britain’s cooking globalised, but the range of fish within these pages stayed narrow.
British boats, including many small vessels, land a diverse mix of locally caught fish and shellfish, but much of that is exported. In contrast, most of the fish eaten today is imported.

Britain’s narrow appetite for fish is often assumed to be a long-standing cultural norm. These recipes suggest otherwise. Viewed through this lens, modern preferences look less like an enduring national trait and more like an outcome of changing supply, trade and food retail. This raises the intriguing possibility that eating habits may be more open to change than previously thought.

One magazine can only reveal so much. Good Housekeeping was written for a particular readership. Its recipes show what was visible and aspirational, not what was prepared and eaten. But unlike specialist fish cookbooks, which are aimed at people already keen on fish, a mass market magazine shows which fish were put in front of ordinary home cooks.

A century ago, British cooks expected the fish on offer to change with the seasons and the catch. Reviving that flexibility, and a taste for local, sustainably caught seafood (such as sardines, pollack or mussels) could benefit our seas and coastal communities. Some suppliers are already pioneering this approach, but it needs to reach the mainstream.

Recipes written with versatility in mind won’t secure the future of Britain’s fish stocks and fishing communities alone, but, combined with thoughtful choices by suppliers and shoppers, they could be a (very enjoyable) step in the right direction.

Ruth H. Thurstan works for The University of Exeter. She received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (grant agreement no. 856488).

articles.title: Shipwrecks can become thriving reefs, but may contain hidden toxic time bombs
articles.author: Nicholas Ray, Doctoral Programmes Manager and Researcher in Aquatic Ecology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Late last year, scientists in Germany published some remarkable findings on a second world war munitions dump in the Baltic Sea. Some may dismiss the dump as hazardous waste, but to marine biologists it was something far more exciting: a thriving ecosystem.

Over the decades, the dump has become home to mussels, crustaceans, fish and marine plant life, creating a full community under the sea. It’s a perfect example of an accidental reef, highlighting nature’s ability to reclaim even dangerous human detritus.

Around the UK coast, there are thousands of famous wrecks. I have had the pleasure of diving on many of them, witnessing first hand how sea creatures turn rusting hulls into habitat. Further afield, deliberate artificial reef projects, from Australia to the Caribbean, are evidence that where structures sink, life follows.
But let’s not romanticise our wrecks. While these structures offer a foothold for life, they can also leak toxic compounds into the oceans.

Not all reefs are born from disaster. Around the world, governments, scientists and conservation groups have deliberately sunk ships, concrete structures and even old underground train carriages to create new marine habitats. These artificial reefs are designed to mimic the ecological functions of natural reefs, boosting biodiversity and providing refuges for overfished species. They also draw scuba divers and recreational fishers, providing economic incentives for people who live nearby.

In the US, the decommissioned aircraft carrier the USS Oriskany was famously sunk to create a tourist attraction off the Florida coast: the “Great Carrier Reef”. In November 2026, an even bigger ship will be sunk nearby: the SS United States, an ocean liner larger than the Titanic.

In Japan, concrete blocks have been used extensively to stabilise coastlines and provide habitat for fish. In Australia, the “rigs-to-reefs” initiative means old oil rigs – too costly to remove – are being left in place to create new ecosystems.
But there’s a fine line between “marine habitat creation” and simply “dumping unwanted stuff”. Poorly planned projects have often done more harm than good.

Perhaps the most infamous case is the Osborne Reef off Florida. In the 1970s, millions of used vehicle tyres were sunk to create a massive reef. But the steel clips holding them soon corroded, and many tyres broke loose and started scouring the seafloor and battering a nearby natural coral reef during storms.
The expensive lesson is that artificial reefs can at best supplement conservation, but they are not a substitute for protecting natural habitats.
Shipwrecks and artificial reefs also bring with them a less visible legacy of metal pollution.

The vast majority of wrecks are made of steel, iron, copper and various other alloys that slowly corrode in seawater. This releases dissolved metals into the surrounding environment, and while iron and steel often rust away harmlessly, other metals can be more problematic.

Copper, zinc, lead, tin and aluminium can leach from hull coatings, machinery, or electrical components. These trace metals and toxic chemicals don’t just wash away. Instead, they accumulate in surrounding sediments and, more worryingly, in the tissues of marine organisms. This is particularly concerning for filter feeders such as mussels and oysters, which can concentrate pollutants and pass them up the food chain to predators – and potentially humans.

In high enough concentrations, these substances become toxic, affecting growth, reproduction and survival. For instance, for many years ship’s hulls were coated with the chemical tributyltin (TBT) to prevent barnacle growth which slows vessels down. However, TBT also caused serious environmental damage: some female dogwhelks developed male sexual organs, for instance, disrupting reproduction cycles in these key coastal molluscs.

The issue is magnified for wrecks that still contain fuel or munitions. Corroding shells and tanks not only release components of explosives but also heavy metals such as mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium, chromium and TNT degradation products.

The Baltic Sea munitions, for example, are slowly leaking toxicants into an already fragile semi-enclosed sea. If fish are still there, how bad can the contamination really be? The problem is that presence does not equal a safe zone. Many toxic metals and explosive residues cause sub-lethal effects that do not immediately drive fish away or kill them outright. Instead, these substances accumulate through the food web. Fish may continue to hang out in contaminated areas while suffering impaired reproduction, altered behaviour, suppressed immune systems, or developmental defects. These effects are ultimately largely invisible without detailed study.

In a semi-enclosed system like the Baltic Sea, limited water exchange exacerbates the problem: contaminants persist longer, sediments act as long-term reservoirs, and chronic exposure becomes unavoidable. What looks like ecological resilience can therefore mask a delayed population collapse, and increased risk to predators, including humans, who potentially consume the fish.
We know that organisms can tolerate pollution in the short term. The question is whether ecosystems can remain functional and safe under decades of continuous, low-level toxic exposure.

The urgent need to create artificial habitats is heightened by the crisis facing natural coral reefs from climate change, ocean acidification, overfishing and pollution. Rising sea temperatures are already triggering mass coral bleaching events.

In this context, wrecks and artificial reefs also serve as accidental laboratories. They show how quickly life will colonise and exploit a new habitat, providing lessons for restoration work elsewhere. But the answer to the reef crisis isn’t simply “sink more ships”.

Artificial reefs should never be seen as a licence to pollute or a shortcut for true conservation. They must complement, not replace, efforts to protect and restore natural habitats. We can’t “offset” destroying an ancient coral reef by sinking an old ship. Conservationists rightly stress the focus must remain on marine protected areas, reducing ocean acidification, tackling overfishing and pollution.
The Baltic Sea munitions “reef” is an accident of history rather than a model for the future. Yes, marine life has flourished there, but it swims in a sea filled with heavy metals and toxins.

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
articles.author: Jaquelyn Jahn, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology, Drexel University
paras: When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons.

Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at SCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.”

I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years.

While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons.

Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme. Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs, Dallas, Laurel Highlands, Muncy, Waymart and Huntingdon, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.
Prison healthcare systems under strain

Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease, and the state’s prison population is getting older, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023.
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year. That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults.

The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.

Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers.

In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour.
Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks

One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men.

This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.

Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “accelerated aging” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected.
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable.
Preparing for a warmer climate

Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.
Jaquelyn Jahn receives funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Arnold Ventures, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

articles.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
articles.author: Peter P. Marra, Dean of The Earth Commons, Professor of Biology and the Environment, Georgetown University
paras: For more than 2,000 years, scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go?

Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species, one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon.
The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable.

Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche, or “arrow storks.” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back.
Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed.

For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view.
Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time.
A century of following birds

Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again.

Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered. That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible.
Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically.

Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations.
At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution.

Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird, an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined.
Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration.
Discovering unknown migrations
More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go.

A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route.

These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity. They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology.

We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds. It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information.
What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map.

Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo. These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia.
In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America.
Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined.
The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem.

Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping. Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations.
They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales.

We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life.
Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history.
North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline.

To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes.

For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young.

But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again.

Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young. Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots, contributing to lower survival.
All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them.

For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small.

More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans. Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data.
Today, millions of bird-watchers contribute observations that, thanks to advances in data science, allow us to watch migration unfold across an entire continent.
We have spent much of our careers documenting the decline of birds, and we know the challenges facing migratory species are formidable. But we also have hope for these creatures’ survival.

Scientists today know more about where migratory birds go, how populations are connected and what they encounter along the way than at any previous point in history. That knowledge is helping to identify where conservation efforts can make a difference for the future.
